text: Pinturas de Tamayo (Pictures of Tamayo) is an orchestral composition in five movements by American composer Steven Stucky, inspired by the paintings of Mexican artist Rufino Tamayo. The work was commissioned by the Chicago Symphony Orchestra and premiered on March 28, 1996, under conductor Michael Gielen at Symphony Center in Chicago. Stucky recalled his first encounter with Tamayo’s art during a visit to the Rufino Tamayo Museum in Mexico City in April 1991, where he was deeply moved by the painting La gran galaxia (The Great Galaxy), describing it as one of the great artistic experiences of his life. Tamayo died in June 1991, just two months after this encounter; since then, Stucky studied his paintings extensively and, when the Chicago Symphony invited him to compose a new work, decided to honor Tamayo by creating an orchestral piece based on his art. The composition has a duration of roughly 22 minutes and is structured in five movements named after Tamayo’s paintings. John von Rhein of the Chicago Tribune criticized the work, stating that translating visual art into sound is difficult and that Stucky’s piece falls short of Gunther Schuller’s Paul Klee studies, calling the color reproductions in the Grainger Ballroom "odious" despite their poor quality. In contrast, Mark Swed of the Los Angeles Times praised the work, noting that Tamayo’s visual impact is matched by Stucky’s colorful orchestral equivalent. Richard Whitehouse of Gramophone observed that the music draws on Tamayo’s imagery but remains understated, highlighting the luminous poise of "Sunset" and the introspective quality of "The Great Galaxy," which serves as an unusually thoughtful conclusion. A recording of Pinturas de Tamayo, performed by Evelyn Glennie and the Singapore Symphony Orchestra under conductor Lan Shui, was released on April 27, 2010, through BIS Records and includes Stucky’s other orchestral works Spirit Voices and the Concerto for Orchestra No. 2.
